place-work.text: Homes and public buildings formed changing neighborhoods, while unfinished copper and local soil evidence reveal particular tasks and environmental questions. Material patterns require context before they become claims about households, authority or regional population.

coordination.text: Concentrated settlement combined monumental construction, agriculture, neighborhoods and specialized work under unequal authority.

evidence-limits.text: A later photograph shows surviving landforms; excavation and contested lake proxies address a broader urban and regional history.

name: Cahokia: city life and the problem of disappearance
place: Mississippi River floodplain near present-day Collinsville, Illinois, United States
geographicPrecision: Cahokia core-site locator; Greater Cahokia and other Mississippian communities are not merged into one state.

interval.label: Selected urban context, c. 1050–1400 CE
interval.note: Urban investigation frame used in the 2020 study; UNESCO describes broader occupation from c800 and an urban peak c1050–1150. The boundary does not assert that Indigenous life ended here.

question: How do we tell the end of an urban center from the end of a people?
summary: Neighborhoods, buildings and skilled work made Cahokia a lived city. Excavated spaces, unfinished copper and local soil evidence explain different parts of that life. A much later photograph and attributed Osage and Peoria accounts keep urban change distinct from the disappearance of Indigenous peoples.

sections.title: Homes within an urban landscape
sections.text: People made a city through more than the building of mounds. In an excavated neighborhood of Greater Cahokia’s East St. Louis precinct, homes were interspersed with public and religious buildings. Betzenhauser and Pauketat compare architectural diversity, density, placement and craft debris to investigate how neighborhoods were created and reconfigured. Identifying a home or workshop requires context, rather than treating every building outline as an identical household. ISAS also connects new pottery forms and limestone with possible ways of preparing maize: an interpretation of material evidence, rather than a complete recovered menu.

citations.locator: Ancient Urbanism; Corn and Cuisine paragraphs

sections.title: Making sheet copper
sections.text: Near Mound 34, skilled making can be investigated through small metal remains. Chastain and colleagues studied eight unfinished copper pieces from earlier excavation backdirt. Their analysis and modern experiments support repeated hammering and annealing, a heating process that softens worked copper for further shaping. Material examination therefore helps explain a sequence of tasks, beyond calling an object a prestige good. The pieces reveal a stage in making sheet, rather than a completed ornament or the identity and working conditions of its maker.

sections.title: Testing an environmental explanation
sections.text: Building, cooking and making used resources. Their effects can be investigated through soils as well as through the objects left behind. Rankin, Barrier and Horsley tested a proposed chain from excessive wood use to erosion and flooding. Their abstract reports a stable buried ground surface around one Cahokia Creek floodplain mound, extending from Mississippian occupation to the nineteenth century. That local finding does not support the expected mechanism there. It also does not settle every environmental question or turn one measured place into a history of the entire region.

sections.title: Later records and living relationships
sections.text: The supplied 1907 print shows a surviving earthwork and planted ground, long after the urban era. Its open view cannot count medieval houses or demonstrate an empty later region. In the Osage Nation’s published preservation account, Andrea Hunter connects ancestral history with the Cahokia and St. Louis area. A university report describes Peoria government representatives discussing research and stewardship during a 2022 visit. These attributed accounts make continuing relationships visible. They do not assign every ancient resident one identity or imply that communities have approved this atlas.

returnPrompt: Distinguish the city’s changing role, a regional population estimate and the continuing history of Indigenous peoples.

deeperReading.title: What one piece cannot reveal
deeperReading.text: The copper study’s material was unfinished and recovered from old backdirt, rather than eight intact ornaments found in use. The authors explain that microstructure records recent working and heating, while earlier cycles can be obscured. Modern replication tests whether a proposed process can produce similar evidence. It does not recover a precise ancient schedule, total work hours or the organization of every craft household. The c.1200 workshop attribution comes through previous field reports, not a fresh date measured on each metal piece.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 1728, 1734–1736: selection and inference limits

deeperReading.title: A soil profile and a lake proxy answer different questions
deeperReading.text: The inherited 2020 White study and 2021 Skousen–Aiuvalasit critique disagree about post-1400 population reconstruction around Horseshoe Lake and the attribution of particular populations. Their previously documented scopes remain in place; no new exact population curve is adopted here. The soil study tests a different mechanism at a different location. Neither evidence stream becomes a direct census, and one local negative result cannot erase all resource pressures. Keep the question, sampled setting and interpretive step connected.

deeperReading.title: Named accounts are not interchangeable
deeperReading.text: Hunter’s geography is presented within an Osage preservation report excerpt. The Peoria visit is described by a university author. Their speakers, purposes and dates differ. Neither is permission to treat all Indigenous histories as one account, and a meeting about research does not establish agreement with every archaeological interpretation.

evidenceReading.title: A later view, a material process and a local environmental test
evidenceReading.introduction: These passages are editorial paraphrases. Photographed form, excavated association and tested inference provide different kinds of explanation; none supplies a complete population history.

items.label: A photograph records its own moment
items.text: The supplied print is dated 1907 and shows a surviving mound in a planted landscape. Archaeological accounts separately describe homes, public buildings and craft activity.
items.interpretation: The visible rows belong to this later view; they do not identify medieval crops, houses or population. Missing structures in a photograph are not proof that a people disappeared.

items.label: Material examination tests a sequence
items.text: The copper researchers combine examination of unfinished pieces with modern replication to support repeated working and heating.
items.interpretation: A process can be supported without recovering an exact schedule, worker identity or completed product. Old backdirt and a workshop-context attribution are not the same as finding an object on a dated household floor.

items.label: An explanation needs its predicted evidence
items.text: Rankin and colleagues report a stable buried surface where a proposed wood-overuse mechanism predicted erosion and flooding.
items.interpretation: That contrast tests a local explanation. It does not prove every landscape was unaffected or resolve the separate Horseshoe Lake population debate. State which place and process the evidence can address.

familyActivity.title: What belongs to the picture, and what needs another source?
steps: Find the surviving mound, a tree and a repeated row pattern in the supplied print. Describe the shapes without naming a crop or an ancient building.

Ask an adult to read the capsule. Sort these claims: rows are visible; researchers infer a copper-working process; the picture counts everyone who lived here. Which is an observation, a supported interpretation and an unsupported claim?
Draw two connected cards labelled working and heating. Use the capsule to explain why a repeated task can be inferred without knowing its exact number of repetitions.
Write a question about a household or neighborhood that this photograph cannot answer. Name the kind of evidence you would seek next.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: this is a 1907 view of a surviving earthwork, not an image of the occupied medieval city. Excavations elsewhere in the urban landscape identify homes among public and religious buildings. A study of eight unfinished copper pieces and modern comparisons supports repeated working and heating, but not an exact cycle count or a named maker. Rows are visible in the print; the working process needs separate material evidence; a complete population count is not supplied. A household question would need contextual excavation or another relevant record, rather than an invented building added to the picture.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or community approval
review.scope: Neighborhoods, material work and local environmental inference, one bounded source-qualified reference, three evidence readings and an answerable later-image/source-capsule task. Six new selected sources consulted on 29 October. The five inherited catalogue/regional/proxy records retain their documented 27 October scopes and access dates. Complete original 1050–1400 interval, identity, claims, old comparison texts, object order and existing image bytes preserved.
limitations: The 2019 neighborhood paper and 2021 soil study were consulted at exposed abstract/metadata level, not complete excavation, profile, sample or household datasets. Spatial and social interpretations do not identify every resident, belief, worker or political relationship.

Copper consultation covers selected introduction/early material-selection and discussion/conclusion text, not full methods, original field records, complete laboratory data or figure pixels. Unfinished pieces from old backdirt do not recover an exact ancient heating schedule, complete cycle count, maker identity or source route.

The LoC catalogue request returned 403 and the inherited Illinois About page timed out; neither was freshly renewed. The 2020/2021 Horseshoe Lake disagreement and UNESCO scope were retained without a new comprehensive consultation. No exact population curve or single cause of urban change adopted.

Osage geography is an attributed selected excerpt from a 2013 preservation report, not a full report or a newly adjudicated affiliation. The 2022 Peoria visit is a university-authored account, not blanket community assent. No external community contact or approval of this atlas is represented.

The unchanged 1907 print was inspected at original detail. Current remote-image parity, photography/printing biography beyond the retained catalogue, precise new geographic points and a reusable archaeological plan remain unverified. No new source figure, plan or micrograph copied or traced. Independent historian/community, real family, human screen-reader and physical-device/print acceptance remain open.
